name: Brothers Mart
description: Trilingual e-commerce platform for a Spanish wholesale grocer: web store, iOS/Android app, admin dashboard and REST API, with Redsys payments, MRW shipping and PDF invoicing.

blocks.text: Brothers Mart is a production e-commerce platform I built for a Spanish wholesale grocery business. Before this, they took orders by phone and wrote invoices by hand. Now customers can order from the web or a mobile app in English, Spanish or Portuguese, and the team runs everything from one admin panel.
The platform is four connected codebases: a Next.js storefront, an Expo/React Native app for iOS and Android, a Next.js admin panel, and a Node.js/Express API behind all three.

blocks.caption: Customer web storefront with URL-synced filters

blocks.text: The business had no online catalog and no way to scale past phone orders. They needed a store that handled Spanish payment rules, local courier shipping, VAT (IVA) pricing and GDPR cookie consent, and an admin panel the team could run without calling a developer.

items: Trilingual catalog (EN/ES/PT). Every product name, slug, description and CMS block is stored per language, with locale-aware URLs.
Redsys card payments on web and mobile, including server-to-server webhook verification and automatic refunds when an order is cancelled.
MRW courier automation. Shipping labels are generated from the admin in one click, and customers get a public tracking page with a 4-step delivery timeline.
IVA price engine. Products are priced with tax included or added on top, and customers can switch between Inc. IVA and Excl. IVA across the whole UI.
Shipping cost calculator based on package dimensions, with provincial and national rates and a free-shipping threshold. It runs client-side, so checkout totals update instantly.
Trilingual PDF invoices with IVA breakdown and coupon lines, generated automatically for every order.
Guest cart and wishlist that survive reloads, then merge with the server cart on login.
GDPR cookie consent with four categories. Nothing is written to local storage without the right consent.
Product catalog filtered by category, subcategory, brand, restaurant type and price, with all filter state kept in the URL so back/forward restores the exact view.
4-step checkout: contact, shipping, billing, payment, with coupon validation and an IVA breakdown.
Redux Toolkit store with a custom sync middleware that pushes cart and wishlist changes to the server and ignores rehydration actions.
PWA support with a service worker and web app manifest.
Built on Expo SDK 54 with file-based routing, NativeWind and Gluestack UI. Five tabs: Home, Explore, Cart, Wishlist, Profile.
Explore screen with infinite scroll, multi-select filters, a price slider and debounced search.
Guest cart saved to AsyncStorage, full server sync once logged in.
Redsys checkout opens in an in-app browser and returns to the app through a deep link.
Universal Links on iOS and intent filters on Android, so product links from the browser open straight in the app.
Automated iOS pipeline on Codemagic: every push to main builds, signs and ships to TestFlight with no manual Xcode steps.
17 sections covering products, categories, brands, coupons, orders, users, blogs, policies, reviews, subscribers and site content.
Analytics dashboard with sales history, order status breakdown, revenue and customer KPIs, and low-stock alerts.
One-click auto-translate on every multilingual field, using the Google Translate API. Long HTML content is split on tag boundaries and all languages are translated in parallel.
Image uploads go straight to Cloudinary with backend-signed requests, so files never pass through the Next.js server.
Rich text editing for blogs and policies, 11 color themes, and list pages that remember search, filters and pagination when you come back from an edit form.
Zod validation with translated error messages.

blocks.caption: Admin dashboard with sales, orders and low-stock alerts

items: Express 5 and TypeScript, with 24 route modules and 17 Mongoose models.
Order creation runs in a MongoDB transaction. It checks stock, deducts it, writes inventory logs, creates the order and updates coupon usage. If any step fails, everything rolls back.
Full Redsys lifecycle: HMAC-SHA256 signed parameters, webhook verification, mobile redirect pages and refunds through the Redsys REST API.
MRW SOAP integration for creating and cancelling shipments and downloading labels, which are then stored on Cloudinary.
Puppeteer renders branded PDF invoices from HTML, using Chromium installed in the Docker image.
Password reset with hashed 6-digit OTPs that expire after 10 minutes, with emails in the user's language.
Role-aware login for the admin panel and the customer apps on shared JWT infrastructure.
Multi-stage Docker build, deployed to a VPS with Docker Compose through GitHub Actions.
Designed the trilingual data model and carried it through all 17 models and all four codebases.
Built the full Redsys payment flow for web and mobile, including webhooks and refunds.
Integrated the MRW SOAP API for shipments, labels and tracking.
Wrote the Redux persistence middleware and the guest-to-account cart merge logic shared by web and mobile.
Built the transactional order flow in MongoDB.
Set up the Puppeteer invoice pipeline and the Docker image that runs it.
Built the auto-translate Server Action and the reusable TranslateButton in the admin panel.
Set up the Codemagic CI/CD pipeline for iOS, including scripts that patch Xcode signing settings.
Built the GDPR cookie consent system and the client-side shipping calculator.
Took the business from phone orders to a working online store that sells across Spain in three languages.
Orders now flow from checkout to payment to shipping label to live tracking without manual steps.
Invoices generate automatically, which removed handwritten paperwork.
The team manages products, orders, pricing, coupons and site content on their own, with no developer needed.
iOS builds ship to TestFlight on every push to main.

name: CarFig Buyer
description: Used car marketplace app for iOS and Android with AI price predictions, comparable-vehicle charts and a Better Deals engine across 6M+ listings. I joined to fix and stabilize the production codebase.

images.alt: Dealearship Inventory, Home & Search Results Screen
images.caption: Dealearship Inventory, Home & Search Result Screen

images.alt: Car detail with price chart & Dealerships Screen
images.caption: Car detail with price chart & Dealerships Screen

blocks.text: CarFig Buyer is a React Native app that helps people shop for used cars. It pulls in more than 6 million live listings from over 80,000 dealerships, and adds price analytics on top: a predicted fair price, a price-versus-mileage chart of similar cars, and a Better Deals list that finds cheaper matches nearby and nationwide.

I joined the team as a bug-fix and stabilization engineer on an existing codebase. My job was to track down broken behavior across state management, UI, and API integration, and fix it so the core features worked reliably.

Buying a used car is stressful, and most listing sites don't tell you whether a price is fair. CarFig gives buyers data to negotiate with. The app also works without an account, so people can search, save favorites and save searches from the first launch.

items: Search with cascading Make, Model and Trim filters, plus year, price, mileage, condition and radius filters. Location comes from a zip code or device GPS.
Smooth scrolling through large result sets with FlashList.
Car detail screen with a photo carousel, full specs and a sticky header.
AI price prediction for each vehicle.
Comparable vehicle scatter chart that ranks the current car against similar listings.
Better Deals list for cheaper matches within about 50 miles and nationwide.
One-tap PDF export of a comparison, built by a server job and shared through the native share sheet.
Favorites and saved searches for guests and signed-in users, migrated to the account on login.
Email and Google sign-in, push notifications through Firebase, and deep links from carfig.com into the app.

blocks.text: React Native 0.80 and React 19, with React Navigation for a three-level navigator. Zustand with AsyncStorage persistence runs seven stores for auth, filters, favorites, guest data, settings and remote config. Networking uses Axios against a REST API with 40+ endpoints. Firebase handles push notifications and Google sign-in, and Codemagic builds the iOS and Android releases.
I owned a long list of production bugs, found the root cause of each, and fixed them without rewriting the app.

items: Fixed the Favorites screen not updating right after add or remove. A stale closure in the Zustand subscription was the cause, so I reworked the optimistic update flow and the selectors.

Fixed guest-to-account migration, which was silently failing on login. Missing awaits and unhandled rejections meant guest favorites and saved searches were lost. The import calls now finish before the app navigates.
Fixed filters being silently dropped from search requests. Version, condition and drivetrain were missing from the params builder, so results ignored them.
Fixed duplicate API calls in infinite scroll when users scrolled back up mid-load, with a loading guard and a correct last-page check.
Fixed the PDF export modal hanging forever. The job ID wasn't passed from the start request into the progress polling loop.
Fixed sticky header flicker on the car detail screen by stopping state updates on every scroll frame.
Fixed the Deals/Analysis tab not defaulting to Analysis when no deals were found, and fixed wrong scroll offsets when switching tabs.
Fixed overlapping toast and snackbar messages by auditing the error paths and standardizing which one shows where.
Fixed random 401 errors caused by the auth interceptor sending the string "null" as the token after logout or on first launch.
Brought favorites, saved searches, filters and PDF export back to working order. These were core features that were broken in production.
Guests who sign up no longer lose their saved cars and searches.
Cut duplicate network requests in search and removed scroll jank on the detail screen.
Removed a class of false 401 errors that were logging users out or breaking API calls.

name: ThunderJaw Restaurant POS
description: Order-to-delivery system for a real restaurant: Electron POS with kitchen display and finance tools, a driver mobile app with live tracking and chat, and a custom API that also powers the restaurant's Alí Doner website and app.

videos.title: Order to delivery
videos.caption: An order created in the POS, assigned to a driver, tracked live and marked delivered from the app.

blocks.text: ThunderJaw is a restaurant management system built for a real food business that runs dine-in, takeaway and delivery at the same time. It covers the full life of an order: taking it, cooking it, sending it out with a driver, tracking the delivery and closing it in the books.

The system has four parts: an Electron desktop POS, a CDN and backup server, a VPS API with WebSocket support, and a React Native app for drivers. The same API serves the restaurant's Alí Doner website and mobile app, so online orders arrive in the POS with no re-entry. It was built by a small team, and I worked across the architecture, backend, sync layer and driver app integration.

blocks.caption: POS terminal with menu, variants and the current order

blocks.text: Orders came in from the counter, the website, the app and delivery platforms like Glovo and Uber Eats, with no single place to see them all. The website and app are a separate project of mine, Alí Doner, built on this same backend. Drivers had no digital workflow, so assignments and status updates were handled by hand. Delivery results never made it back into the POS automatically. And the owners had no clear view of cash, payroll, purchases or fleet costs. Off-the-shelf POS tools either skipped delivery or couldn't handle custom driver dispatch.

items: One order queue for every channel. Local, web, app and third-party orders show up in the same place, with ticket prefixes so staff know the source at a glance.
Kitchen display with color-coded timers that change as orders get older, based on configurable thresholds.
Delivery board with a live map of driver locations.
One-click driver assignment, synced to the driver's phone.
Driver app with a mapped route, distance and ETA, per-order chat with the restaurant, and one-tap Delivered or Cancelled.
Delivery results sync back to the POS on their own, including payment status and delivery time.
Menu management with variants, complement groups, set menus and allergens.
Role-based permissions per module and per function for admin, kitchen, manager and staff.
Finance tools for cash and card reports, worker payroll, vehicle maintenance, supplier purchases, expenses and cash-outs.
English and Spanish interface, and a first-run wizard that connects the POS to its PostgreSQL database with no hardcoded config.

images.alt: Delivery board with live driver map
images.caption: Delivery board and live driver map

items: Desktop POS: Electron, React and TypeScript with a local PostgreSQL database managed by Knex migrations.

VPS API: Express and WebSocket server that sits between the POS and the driver app. It handles driver and admin auth, live location, delivery chat and web order intake, and it also serves the Alí Doner website and mobile app.
CDN and backup server: handles image uploads and runs automated database and image backups.
Driver app: Expo and React Native, with background location tracking and push notifications.

blocks.text: Sync is polling-based, with no message broker. The POS pushes driver profiles and assignments to the VPS on every change, then checks the VPS every 10 seconds for delivery updates and new web orders. Driver locations travel over WebSocket and are broadcast to every connected client. Two PostgreSQL databases (POS and VPS) with 30+ tables share matching migration sets, with soft deletes and audit timestamps throughout.

blocks.caption: POS, VPS, CDN server and driver app

items: Order list that refreshes every 5 seconds, with an unread chat badge and a full item summary.
Route drawn on a native map using the Google Routes API v2, with distance and ETA.
Background location tracking that ignores small movements under 8 meters, so a parked driver doesn't flood the server.
Push notifications for new assignments and chat messages.
Built and shipped through EAS and Codemagic.

images.alt: Route map with distance and ETA
images.caption: Route, distance and ETA

items: Separate auth for drivers, admins and web customers. Admin WebSockets must authenticate within 8 seconds of connecting.
Customer push notifications through Expo on every order status change.
Per-order delivery chat saved to PostgreSQL and broadcast live.
Database dumps with pg_dump every 30 minutes, and a daily image archive at 2 AM.
Backup pruning that keeps the 8 newest dumps plus the latest dump from each of the last 2 days.
Structured logging with Winston, using a separate log file per job.

blocks.text: This was a team project. These are the areas where I did the most work:

items: Designed the two-way sync between the POS and the VPS, including the polling loops and the sync manager.
Built the CDN and backup server: scheduled pg_dump jobs, backup pruning, and image sync to the VPS.
Designed and built VPS API routes, including the WebSocket server with its auth handshake, location broadcast and chat storage.
Designed the database schemas and Knex migrations for both the POS and VPS databases.
Integrated the driver app: background location with drift filtering, push registration and Google Routes API v2 routing.
Built the role-based permission system in the POS.
Built the finance views for workers, vehicles, purchases, expenses, incomes and cash-outs.
Web and app orders go straight into the kitchen queue with no re-entry.
Drivers went from no digital tools to a full mobile workflow: assignment, route, chat and delivery confirmation.
Backups every 30 minutes cap the worst-case data loss at about 30 minutes.
Payroll, purchases, fleet and expense tracking moved from spreadsheets into the POS.
Ticket prefixes (local, W-, A-, platform) tell kitchen and delivery staff where each order came from.

blocks.title: Order to delivery
blocks.caption: From a new order in the POS to a confirmed delivery on the driver's phone.

name: Alí Doner
description: Direct ordering platform for a kebab restaurant in Spain: a Next.js website, an Expo mobile app and an admin CMS, running on the same backend as the restaurant's ThunderJaw POS.

images.alt: Favourites, Profile & Initial Order Type Screen
images.caption: Favourites, Profile & Initial Order Type Screen

blocks.text: Alí Doner is a kebab restaurant in Rivas-Vaciamadrid, Spain. I built its customer platform with a partner: a Next.js website, a React Native app for iOS and Android, and an admin panel, all running on one REST backend.

Customers can browse the menu, order for delivery or pickup, customize items, save favorites, check past orders and message support in Spanish or English. The owner manages all of it from the admin panel without touching code. Everything runs on the same backend as the restaurant's ThunderJaw POS, so web and app orders land in the kitchen queue on their own.

The restaurant wanted its own ordering channel instead of depending on delivery marketplaces that take a commission. The owner also needed to change hero images, opening hours, FAQs, allergen info, announcements and legal pages without a developer. And the platform had to plug into the backend the restaurant's POS already used, so online orders would land in the kitchen queue on their own.
Other requirements: accept delivery orders only inside a defined zone (a polygon, not a simple radius), support Spanish and English throughout, and meet GDPR rules for a Spanish audience.

items: Menu with categories, subcategories, products, discount badges and allergen indicators. Category and search links work directly from the URL.
Delivery or pickup chosen upfront. Delivery addresses are checked against the zone polygon with Google Maps, so out-of-range customers find out before they fill the cart.
Cart with variants, complement groups, set menus, discounts and an IVA breakdown.
Three-step checkout: address and contact, payment (cash or card on delivery), then a summary with legal consent.
Accounts with email verification before ordering, silent token refresh, password reset, order history, saved favorites and profile settings.
Dark and light themes with no flash on load, and an ES/EN language toggle.
Legal, About, FAQ and allergen pages all render from the CMS, with nothing hardcoded.
Catalog with a category bar, search and favorite toggles.
Product screen with variant selection and a complement builder, plus a combo builder for multi-page set menus.
Cart saved on the device, with haptic feedback and the full IVA breakdown.
Same three-step checkout as the web. The order payload is ported from the web version, so both channels send identical data.
Delivery zone check through a server-side geocoding proxy, so the Google Maps key never reaches the client, followed by a polygon test on the device.
Push notifications for order status, registered only after the customer gives marketing consent.
One-tap reorder from history, in-app support messages and location-based address autofill.
Built with EAS and Codemagic.
Dashboard with customer counts, open support tickets, unread messages, web and app order totals, pending orders and menu counts.

CMS for the hero slider, footer and social links, Terms, Privacy Policy, FAQs, About, Contact and Allergen pages. Each field has side-by-side Spanish and English editors with a one-click translate button.
Settings for the logo, restaurant name, opening hours, an announcement bar shown on the website and the app, app store links, and a maintenance mode switch.
Customer list with filters for active, unverified and deleted accounts, plus search by name or email.
Support inbox with threaded conversations, replies, open and resolved status, and a live unread badge over WebSocket.
All three apps use one versioned REST API, the same VPS backend that powers the restaurant's ThunderJaw POS.
Orders are tagged by source (web or app, delivery or pickup) and get W- or A- ticket numbers, so the kitchen sees where each one came from.
Customers use access and refresh tokens. On mobile, simultaneous 401 errors share a single refresh request. Admin uses its own token and secret.
Content flows from the admin into a site content table, and the web and mobile apps load it on start. The apps wait for the content before rendering, which is also how maintenance mode works.

blocks.text: I built this with a partner and worked on these areas:

items: Admin panel architecture and every CMS page, including the BlockNote editor, the bilingual field design and the auto-translate flow.
Admin dashboard stats and the support inbox with live unread badges.
Website architecture: auth with silent refresh, cart pricing logic, delivery zone validation and the site content gate.
The mobile cart and pricing engine, ported from the web so both send the same order format.
Polygon-based delivery zone checks on web and mobile.
The 3-step mobile checkout.
Localization across all three apps.
Push notification registration tied to GDPR consent.
The theme system: dark and light with no flash on the web, dark-only on mobile.
Three production apps serving real customers of a live restaurant.
The restaurant takes orders directly, with no marketplace commission.
The owner edits every text, image and legal page in Spanish and English without a developer.
Customers learn right away whether their address is in the delivery zone, so fewer orders get rejected after checkout.
Web and app orders go straight into the ThunderJaw POS kitchen queue with no re-entry.
GDPR covered end to end: email verification, consent-gated push tokens, account deletion and token invalidation on password change.

name: Dynamic Subscription Planner
description: ML-powered tool that segments chauffeur-service customers with K-Means and generates a personalized discount and free-trip plan for each member in seconds, with the full calculation shown.

videos.title: Plan generation
videos.caption: Looking up a member, seeing their cluster and the step-by-step formula behind their plan.

images.alt: Radar chart comparing the three clusters
images.caption: Cross-cluster comparison

blocks.text: The client is a premium chauffeur and airport-transfer service in Saudi Arabia and the GCC. I built a web app for them that studies how each customer travels, sorts customers into three groups with machine learning, and then calculates a personal subscription plan: a discount percentage and a number of free trips.
I designed and built the whole thing myself: the data pipeline, the model, the REST API and the dashboard.

blocks.alt: Generated subscription plan for a member
blocks.caption: A generated plan with cluster, discount, free trips and the formula breakdown

blocks.text: Every member got the same subscription offer. Frequent, high-spending travelers received the same rewards as people who rode twice a year, so loyalty went unrewarded and the best customers were a churn risk. There was also no way to spot who was about to upgrade or drift away.

Account managers decided discounts by reading individual histories whenever they had time, with no consistent method. The business wanted something repeatable and explainable that could produce a plan for any member in seconds.

items: Each customer's trip history is reduced to three numbers: Recency (days since the last trip), Frequency (total trips) and Monetary value (total spend), plus their preferred service type and route.
K-Means with k=3 groups members into Platinum (frequent, high value), Gold (premium but infrequent) and Silver (occasional).

A custom scoring formula turns each member's numbers into a benefit score: B = (wM × Mnorm) + (wF × Fnorm) − (wR × Rnorm). Each cluster has its own weights, and the result is bounded to set a discount and a free-trip count.
The dashboard shows the plan next to the exact formula with the member's real values filled in.
Plan lookup by membership ID, showing the cluster, a donut chart of the discount and a visual of the free trips.
Live data intake. Submitting new transactions in the UI reruns the whole pipeline: clean, build RFM, retrain, refresh.
Cluster insights dashboard with a tab for each cluster, bar charts of its typical behavior, a radar chart comparing all three clusters and a suggested engagement strategy for each tier.
Explainable results. Every recommendation shows which weights were used and how the final numbers came out, so account managers can defend them to customers.
Three tiers: Platinum gets up to 25% off and 5 free trips, Gold gets 20% and 3 trips, Silver gets 15% and 2 trips.

blocks.text: A Streamlit front end calls a FastAPI back end over HTTP, and the back end reads and writes a CSV data layer. The API has three endpoints: POST /data to add transactions, POST /recommend to generate a plan and GET /get-rfm to read the RFM table. Pydantic validates requests, scikit-learn runs K-Means and scaling, pandas and NumPy handle the data, joblib saves the model and Plotly draws the charts.

items: Designed and built everything from the data pipeline to the model, the API and the UI.
Designed the weighted scoring formula, with separate weight sets per cluster for the discount and for the free-trip count.
Built the cleaning step for messy real-world data: typos, mixed date formats and text in numeric columns.
Structured the FastAPI back end in layers (models, services, routes, main) following SOLID principles.
Designed the results screen so the formula and values are visible next to every plan.
Built the retraining loop that runs on every new data submission.
Built the analytics dashboard with its radar and bar charts.
Styled the Streamlit app with custom CSS to match the client's brand.
Plans that used to need manual review by an account manager now appear in seconds.
Three defined tiers with clear benefits, so rewards now follow customer behavior.
Every recommendation can be traced back to a member's raw RFM numbers.
The model updates itself as new transactions come in, with no data scientist needed.
The segmentation can grow to more tiers, and reward rules can change without rebuilding the system.

name: CalAI Backend
description: FastAPI backend for a calorie-tracking mobile app. Gemini analyzes meal photos, a diet engine builds plans from body data, and one API handles Apple and Google Play subscriptions.

videos.title: Photo to nutrition breakdown
videos.caption: Uploading a meal photo, getting the food items and macros back, then fixing a wrong guess.

blocks.text: CalAI is the backend for a Flutter app that tracks calories and nutrition. A user takes a photo of a meal and gets back every food item, its estimated weight, and the full macro breakdown. The app then tracks the day's intake against a plan built from the user's own body data.
I was the only backend engineer. I designed and built the whole API, the database, the AI pipeline and the subscription system for both iOS and Android.

items: Logging food by hand is slow, and most people quit within weeks. A photo takes a second.
A flat 2,000 calorie target ignores gender, age, weight, height and activity. Plans need to come from the person's actual body data.
A cross-platform app needs subscription checks for Apple StoreKit 2 and the Google Play API, which work in completely different ways.

AI food analysis. Photos go to Gemini 2.0 Flash through Vertex AI. The model lists each food, estimates its weight in grams, returns macros per 100 g, scores the meal's health from 1 to 10 and writes a short overview. The backend scales the numbers by grams and totals the meal.

Fix flow. If the AI got something wrong, the user can type a correction like "that's brown rice, not white rice." The backend reloads the original photo, reruns Gemini with the earlier result and the correction, and updates the meal.

Personal diet plans. From gender, birth date, height, weight, goal (lose, gain or maintain), workout frequency and target weight, it works out BMR with the Mifflin-St Jeor equation, applies an activity factor, adds a deficit or surplus for the goal, and splits calories 25/50/25 across protein, carbs and fat. It accepts metric and imperial units. Changing any body detail recalculates the plan.

Daily macro tracking. Each day's remaining macros start from the plan on the first log. Logging a meal subtracts from them and deleting a meal adds them back. A streak counter resets if the user skips more than a day.

Ingredient search and manual entry. A 50,000+ row nutrition CSV loads into memory at startup. Users can search with pagination, add an ingredient to a meal by grams, change quantities or remove items, and the totals update straight away.
Accounts. Email and password sign-up, Google and Apple sign-in, JWT access and refresh tokens, password reset by emailed 6-digit code that expires in 15 minutes, and soft-delete for accounts.
Subscriptions for iOS and Android, described below.
Apple: the backend signs an ES256 JWT, calls the App Store Server API, decodes the signed transaction, checks the expiry and saves the subscription.
Google Play: it validates the purchase token through the Play Developer API, acknowledges the purchase and stores the expiry.
Google lifecycle events (renewals, cancellations, grace periods) arrive through a Pub/Sub webhook. They run as background tasks, so the endpoint answers Google right away.

blocks.text: FastAPI on Python 3.11 with PostgreSQL through SQLAlchemy. Code is layered: routes call services, which use utilities and schemas, and FastAPI dependency injection handles database sessions and auth. Business logic sits in service classes (user, food analysis, Google Play, ingredients), which keeps the routes thin. The API is versioned under /api/v0 and /api/v1, with /api/latest pointing to v0. Meal images are stored in Supabase Storage, and their URLs are encrypted with Fernet before they go into the database. Passwords use bcrypt.
I was the sole backend engineer. I built:

items: The Gemini pipeline. I wrote the prompt so the model returns consistent JSON, with temperature 0.3, a fixed seed and a forced JSON response type. I wrapped the synchronous Vertex AI SDK in a thread pool so it doesn't block the event loop under load.
The BMR, TDEE and macro engine, including unit conversion and automatic plan recalculation on any body-data change.
Apple StoreKit 2 and Google Play verification, including the JWT signing, the JWS decoding and the Pub/Sub webhook.
The v1 additions: Apple Sign In, the AI fix flow and ingredient search and editing. v1 extends v0 without breaking existing app versions.
Security: Fernet-encrypted image URLs, bcrypt hashing, two-token JWT rotation and soft-delete accounts.
The database design: 8 PostgreSQL tables with relationships, cascade rules and indexes, plus a connection pool sized for many parallel AI analyses.
The versioned API structure that lets v0 and v1 change independently.
Logging a meal now takes one photo, instead of searching and typing for each food.
The backend is set up to run up to 100 image analyses at the same time, using a 100-worker thread pool and a semaphore.
Subscriptions work on both stores from one backend, so the app can earn revenue on iOS and Android.
Every user gets a plan calculated from their own body data and goal.
The daily macro ledger starts safely on the first log, so retries and logins from several devices don't corrupt a user's day.
